Observation-level burn-probability model — design

From the canonical-team term set to the reduced 129-term elastic-net design (MapBiomas Argentina Fuego, Collection 1, step 02)

Author

Iván Barberá

Published

June 22, 2026

0.1 What this notebook is

This is the single, end-to-end record of how the Collection-1 observation-level burn-probability model was designed. The story runs in one direction:

  1. Term design (the greedy start). We first wrote down the maximal design we were willing to evaluate in Google Earth Engine — the canonical-team set, 427 terms: 21 focal spectral features, 40 previous-year MapBiomas-mosaic bands, and six interaction blocks built on top of them. The strategy was deliberately greedy: give the elastic net as much flexibility as the GEE compute budget allows and let regularization sort it out.
  2. The convergence problem. glmnet’s elastic-net path was slow to converge on that design. The diagnosis below shows the cause was numerical, not statistical: a heavily collinear design matrix makes coordinate descent crawl in the ill-conditioned low-\(\lambda\) tail.
  3. The reduction protocol. We then reduced the design from 427 → 129 terms with a specific, reproducible protocol — pairwise-correlation pruning, an exact-linear- combination argument (which is how MIRBI and the tasseled-cap trio leave), a multivariate VIF screen, and a final fitting-config fix. Everything in Part III below runs on the full 5.72M-observation training set at render time.
  4. The final design + fitting config, matching workflow/02-model_fitting.R term-for-term (that script is the source of truth).

This notebook renders on the full data. The correlation, separability, eigenvalue, and VIF chunks read all five region tables (collection-01/data/training_observations_*_v1.csv, ~3.8 GB, ~5.72M obs) and compute on the complete set. It is therefore a heavy render (several minutes, several GB of RAM). The big matrices are rm()-ed and gc()-ed between sections to keep the peak bounded.

1 Part I — Term design (the greedy start)

1.1 Scope and motivation

MapBiomas Argentina Fuego Collection 1 produces annual burned-area maps for all of Argentina over 1999–2025 using Landsat C2 SR. The pipeline relies on a per-observation (pixel-date) burn-probability classifier evaluated for every Landsat scene intersecting the territory and the time window. That prediction step is the cost driver: the model is applied many billions of times, so the structure must be cheap to evaluate in GEE.

Collection 0 (Patagonia pilot) used a logistic regression with 40 terms per vegetation type, four fire-relevant indices (NBR, NBR2, MIRBI, NDVI), and a hand-picked interaction set that included custom annual min/max summaries and \(\Delta\) values. Collection 1 keeps logistic regression — for the same compute reasons — but rebalances the design:

  • More focal flexibility: many spectral features per observation instead of 4.
  • Previous-year context from MapBiomas: replace custom-computed annual summaries with the official MapBiomas Argentina annual mosaic of year \(y-1\), which provides phenologically informed composites at no extra preprocessing cost.
  • No deltas: with rich pairwise interactions, monotonic effects and the inherent non-linearity of the logistic link absorb most of what \(\Delta\) terms did in Collection 0. A 2-way interaction in \(\eta\) already implies a roughly 3-way effect on the predicted probability.
  • Flexibility over interpretability: this model is for prediction, not inference. Collinearity is acceptable in principle and addressed by an elastic-net fit (tuning both \(\lambda\) and \(\alpha\)). The catch — that “acceptable” collinearity still has to be fittable in finite time — is the entire subject of Part II.
  • Stratification: one model per region × vegetation type (using the MapBiomas LULC of year \(y-1\), reclassified into a few coarse fire-classes), as in Collection 0.

The original design constraint was roughly 200–300 terms per linear predictor to keep the GEE compute graph small. Below ~200 we lose flexibility; much above ~300 the graph grows enough to slow full-territory prediction without obvious gains. The reduction in Part III lands the final model comfortably inside that envelope, at 129 terms.

1.2 Why the MapBiomas annual mosaic (instead of custom summaries)

In Collection 0 we computed our own per-pixel annual minimum and maximum of each fire index with a robust order-statistic rule. That was viable for one region × four indices but does not scale: doing the same over all of Argentina, for two years per focal year (\(y-1\) in addition to \(y\)), with many more features, would multiply preprocessing cost considerably.

The MapBiomas Argentina annual mosaic already provides, for every year, a coherent set of pixel-level composites:

  • median, dry-season median, wet-season median, minimum, and within-year standard deviation of the six optical bands;
  • the same statistics for a broad set of vegetation and fire-relevant indices (NDVI, NDWI, EVI2, SAVI, GCVI, NDFI, SEFI, WEFI, …);
  • SMA endmember fractions (GV, GVS, NPV, soil, shade, cloud);
  • topographic information.

Using this mosaic instead of recomputing custom summaries removes a heavy preprocessing step, ensures consistency with the LULC product used for stratification, offers seasonal composites (wet, dry) we never had in Collection 0, and provides physically interpretable derived layers (NPV as a fuel-load proxy, NDFI as a fire/disturbance signal). The trade-off: we cannot freely define the summaries; we choose among what the mosaic exposes.

1.3 Which previous-year summaries (median, wet, sd — and the dry debate)

A previous-year summary is useful only insofar as it describes the stable spectral state of the pixel — the baseline against which the focal observation is compared. Summaries that move sharply when the pixel itself was disturbed in \(y-1\) are confounded by exactly the kind of signal we want to detect later.

Subscript Meaning
\(X_t\) Value of feature \(X\) at the focal observation (pixel-date)
\(X_{\text{med}}\) MapBiomas mosaic median of \(X\) in year \(y(t) - 1\)
\(X_{\text{wet}}\) MapBiomas mosaic wet-season median of \(X\) in year \(y(t) - 1\)
\(X_{\text{dry}}\) MapBiomas mosaic dry-season median of \(X\) in year \(y(t) - 1\)
\(X_{\text{sd}}\) MapBiomas mosaic within-year standard deviation of \(X\) in year \(y(t) - 1\)

The canonical-team design carried all four summaries (\(\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{dry}, \text{sd}\)). The reasoning for and against each:

  • \(\text{med}\) — robust central tendency. Insensitive to a single fire event unless the fire affected a large fraction of the year’s images. Keep.
  • \(\text{wet}\) — median of wet-season images. The wet season precedes the fire season, so a fire in \(y-1\) generally occurs after the wet composite is laid down: the most fire-robust baseline in the mosaic. Keep.
  • \(\text{sd}\) — within-year variability. Contextualizes change: pixels with naturally high \(\text{sd}\) should be judged against a more permissive burn threshold. Keep.
  • \(\text{dry}\) — the dry season is the fire season, so a \(y-1\) fire contaminates the dry composite in the same direction as the future fire we want to detect (dry NDVI drops, dry SWIR rises). For pixels that did not burn in \(y-1\) (the majority) it still carries peak- senescence / end-of-season fuel signal, so the canonical-team set kept it and let the net decide. In the reduction (Part III) it is dropped from the interaction blocks (kept only as a main effect) because it is partly redundant with \(\text{med}\) and risks bias on previously-burned pixels.

We never used \(\text{amp}\) (max − min, inflated by either fire or normal phenology) or bare \(\text{min}\)/\(\text{max}\) (which only supported \(\Delta\) features we dropped).

1.4 Spectral feature equations

The base focal feature set is 17 features (six optical bands + 11 indices); the canonical-team proposal extends this to 21 by adding AFRI, kNDVI, EVI2, NIRv.

Group Feature Definition
Optical BLUE, GREEN, RED, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2 Surface-reflectance bands
Fire \(\text{NBR}\) \((\text{NIR} - \text{SWIR2}) / (\text{NIR} + \text{SWIR2})\)
Fire \(\text{NBR2}\) \((\text{SWIR1} - \text{SWIR2}) / (\text{SWIR1} + \text{SWIR2})\)
Fire \(\text{MIRBI}\) \(10\,\text{SWIR2} - 9.8\,\text{SWIR1} + 2\)
Fire \(\text{NDVI}\) \((\text{NIR} - \text{RED}) / (\text{NIR} + \text{RED})\)
Tasseled-cap \(\text{TCB}\) \(0.3029\,\text{BLUE} + 0.2786\,\text{GREEN} + 0.4733\,\text{RED} + 0.5599\,\text{NIR} + 0.5080\,\text{SWIR1} + 0.1872\,\text{SWIR2}\)
Tasseled-cap \(\text{TCG}\) \(-0.2941\,\text{BLUE} - 0.2430\,\text{GREEN} - 0.5424\,\text{RED} + 0.7276\,\text{NIR} + 0.0713\,\text{SWIR1} - 0.1608\,\text{SWIR2}\)
Tasseled-cap \(\text{TCW}\) \(0.1511\,\text{BLUE} + 0.1973\,\text{GREEN} + 0.3283\,\text{RED} + 0.3407\,\text{NIR} - 0.7117\,\text{SWIR1} - 0.4559\,\text{SWIR2}\)
Aux. moisture \(\text{NDMI}\) \((\text{NIR} - \text{SWIR1}) / (\text{NIR} + \text{SWIR1})\)
Aux. snow \(\text{NDSI}\) \((\text{GREEN} - \text{SWIR1}) / (\text{GREEN} + \text{SWIR1})\)
Aux. sparse veg \(\text{SAVI}\) \([(\text{NIR} - \text{RED}) / (\text{NIR} + \text{RED} + L)]\,(1 + L)\), \(L = 0.5\)
Aux. open water \(\text{NDWI}\) \((\text{GREEN} - \text{NIR}) / (\text{GREEN} + \text{NIR})\)
Aux. aerosol-free \(\text{AFRI}\) \((\text{NIR} - 0.5\,\text{SWIR2}) / (\text{NIR} + 0.5\,\text{SWIR2})\)
Aux. veg. kernel \(\text{kNDVI}\) \(\tanh(\text{NDVI}^2)\)
Aux. enhanced veg \(\text{EVI2}\) \(2.5\,(\text{NIR} - \text{RED}) / (\text{NIR} + 2.4\,\text{RED} + 1)\)
Aux. NIR veg \(\text{NIRv}\) \(\text{NIR} \times \text{NDVI}\)

Notes: tasseled-cap coefficients are Baig et al. (2014) for Landsat 8 OLI. MIRBI is in the raw Trigg & Flasse (2001) orientation; it increases after fire (opposite sign of NBR, NBR2, NDVI). NDWI here is McFeeters (1996), distinct from NDMI (Gao 1996). AFRI is AFRI-2100 (Karnieli et al. 2001, Eq. 11a); kNDVI uses the RBF-kernel form (Camps-Valls et al. 2021); EVI2 is the blue-band- free EVI (Jiang et al. 2008); NIRv is Badgley et al. (2017).

Note two facts that drive the whole reduction in Part III:

  • \(\text{MIRBI} = 10\,\text{SWIR2} - 9.8\,\text{SWIR1} + 2\) is an exact linear function of two raw bands we keep.
  • \(\text{TCB}, \text{TCG}, \text{TCW}\) are exact linear functions of the six raw bands.
  • \(\text{NBR}, \text{NBR2}, \text{NDMI}\) are ratios of pairs of raw bands — near-functions of them (nonlinear, so not exact, but strongly collinear).

Previous-year variables beyond the six optical bands, taken directly from the mosaic: NDVI and NDWI (same formulas as focal), NPV (non-photosynthetic vegetation fraction from SMA — fine-fuel proxy), and NDFI (Normalized Difference Fraction Index, Souza et al. 2005 — disturbance signal).

1.5 The canonical-team design — 427 terms

The linear predictor is \[\Pr(y_{c,t} = 1) = \sigma\!\Big(\alpha_{k[c]} + \sum_{j} \beta_{j,k[c]}\, x_{j,c,t}\Big),\] with \(k[c]\) the vegetation cluster of pixel \(c\) in year \(y-1\) and \(\sigma\) the logistic function. The canonical-team set organizes the terms into six blocks:

Block Description Count
1 Focal raw (21 features) 21
2 Prev-year raw (10 vars × 4 summaries) 40
3 Focal × focal pairwise, \(\binom{21}{2}\) 210
4 Same-band prev × focal (8 vars × 4 summaries) 32
5 Prev context × focal fire indices (\(4\times4\times4 - 4\)) 60
6 Prev context × focal fire bands (\(4\times4\times4\)) 64
Total 427

The modeling claim behind blocks 5–6 is that the meaning of a focal fire-index value depends on the previous-year vegetation context: a low \(\text{NBR}_t\) in a high-NPV, low-NDFI pixel (heavy dead biomass, recently disturbed) is far more likely to be fire than the same \(\text{NBR}_t\) in a low-NPV, high-NDFI pixel. Block 3 (the 210 focal pairs) carries most of the raw flexibility. This was the greedy maximum: maximal expressiveness within a ~15-node GEE graph (see §[GEE]). The problem was getting it to fit.

2 Part II — The convergence problem

02-model_fitting.R’s elastic-net search was slow to converge on the 427-term design — some classes took many hours per \(\alpha\), occasionally not finishing. Two hypotheses:

  • Statistical: not enough signal / too many obs, intrinsically hard problem.
  • Numerical: the design matrix is so collinear that glmnet’s coordinate descent crawls in the ill-conditioned, low-\(\lambda\) tail (where the active set is large), and a coarse \(\lambda\) grid gives poor warm starts.

The leading suspect was numerical. The canonical-team design expands 21 focal features + 40 mosaic bands into 427 terms via pairwise products and curated crosses. If the raw inputs are already strongly correlated, every interaction block inherits and amplifies that redundancy — products of collinear factors are even more collinear than the factors. Coordinate descent on a near-singular Gram matrix converges geometrically slowly.

Part III tests that hypothesis directly (it is correct) and acts on it in two ways: remove the removable redundancy (exact linear combinations and duplicated axes add columns but no information, so they only hurt conditioning) and keep the irreducible redundancy (bands + their ratio-indices are intentionally near-collinear; that residual is what the elastic-net ridge component, \(\alpha<1\), is designed to absorb). The leftover knob — glmnet’s convergence tolerance — turns out to be the single biggest speed lever (§[Fitting]).

3 Part III — The collinearity-reduction protocol

Everything below executes on the full data. The protocol, in order:

  1. Focal mains: pairwise correlation + univariate separability → keep 12 → drop MIRBI and the tasseled-cap trio as exact linear combinations → 11 focal mains.
  2. Prev-year mains: pairwise correlation → drop the duplicated visible bands → 32.
  3. Focal × focal interactions: prune on centered-factor products → 22.
  4. Prev × focal interactions: keep the curated B4–B6 blocks, restricted to median + sd → 64.
  5. Multivariate VIF + the intentional near-rank-deficiency (eigenvalues of the bands + ratio-indices block), the redundancy we keep on purpose.

3.1.1 Correlation helpers (big-data friendly)

cor_fast standardizes columns once and forms crossprod / (n-1) — a single BLAS matmul, far faster than per-pair cor() at millions of rows. Rows with any non-finite value in the group are dropped (complete-case within the group). cor_spearman ranks each column first (robust to the indices’ non-linearity). find_redundant is the iterative pairwise pruner from caret::findCorrelation, reimplemented.

Code 
cor_fast <- function(M) {
  ok <- is.finite(rowSums(M)); M <- M[ok, , drop = FALSE]
  attr_n <- nrow(M); M <- scale(M)
  C <- crossprod(M) / (attr_n - 1)
  C[!is.finite(C)] <- NA
  attr(C, "n_used") <- attr_n
  C
}
cor_spearman <- function(M) {
  R <- apply(M, 2, function(x) frank(x, ties.method = "average", na.last = "keep"))
  cor_fast(R)
}
high_pairs <- function(C, thresh = 0) {
  ut <- which(upper.tri(C), arr.ind = TRUE)
  d  <- data.table(var1 = rownames(C)[ut[, 1]], var2 = colnames(C)[ut[, 2]], r = C[ut])
  d  <- d[is.finite(r)][abs(r) >= thresh][order(-abs(r))]
  d[, r := round(r, 3)][]
}
# Display-only sanitizer for corrplot: clamp tiny floating-point overshoot back into [-1,1]
# and zero out any non-finite cell (e.g. a near-zero-variance mosaic column). Does NOT touch
# the matrices used for the numeric tables above.
for_plot <- function(C) { C <- round(C, 6); C[!is.finite(C)] <- 0; pmax(pmin(C, 1), -1) }
# Greedy redundancy pruning. protect: never dropped. score: higher = keep (drops the
# lower-scoring member of the worst pair); if NULL, drops the higher-mean-|r| (globally
# more-redundant) member.
find_redundant <- function(C, thresh, protect = character(0), score = NULL) {
  A <- abs(C); diag(A) <- NA; drop <- character(0)
  repeat {
    keep <- setdiff(rownames(A), drop)
    sub  <- A[keep, keep, drop = FALSE]
    if (!any(sub > thresh, na.rm = TRUE)) break
    mx   <- which(sub == max(sub, na.rm = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
    cand <- keep[c(mx[1], mx[2])]; free <- setdiff(cand, protect)
    if (length(free) == 0L) { A[cand[1], cand[2]] <- A[cand[2], cand[1]] <- NA; next }
    if (length(free) == 1L) { drop <- c(drop, free); next }
    loser <- if (!is.null(score)) free[which.min(score[free])]
             else free[which.max(c(mean(sub[free[1], ], na.rm = TRUE),
                                   mean(sub[free[2], ], na.rm = TRUE)))]
    drop <- c(drop, loser)
  }
  drop
}

3.2.1 Univariate separability (burned vs unburned)

How well does each index alone separate burned from unburned? Headline is the AUC (Mann–Whitney, threshold-free): 0.5 = none, 1 = perfect; sep \(= |\text{AUC}-0.5|\cdot 2\). This needs the burned label (absent from dt), so it does a fresh lightweight full read of burned + the 21 focal columns.

Code 
sep_cols <- c("burned", FOCAL21)
sepdt <- rbindlist(lapply(REGIONS, function(reg) {
  message("  reading burned+focal from ", basename(obs_csv(reg)), " ...")
  fread(obs_csv(reg), select = sep_cols)
}), use.names = TRUE)

auc1 <- function(x, y) {
  ok <- is.finite(x); x <- x[ok]; y <- y[ok]
  n1 <- as.numeric(sum(y == 1L)); n0 <- as.numeric(sum(y == 0L))
  if (n1 == 0 || n0 == 0) return(NA_real_)
  r <- frank(x, ties.method = "average")
  (sum(r[y == 1L]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
yb  <- as.integer(sepdt$burned)
sep <- rbindlist(lapply(FOCAL21, function(f) {
  x  <- sepdt[[f]]; ok <- is.finite(x)
  a  <- auc1(x, yb)
  mb <- mean(x[ok & yb == 1L]); mu <- mean(x[ok & yb == 0L])
  vb <- var(x[ok & yb == 1L]);  vu <- var(x[ok & yb == 0L])
  n1 <- sum(ok & yb == 1L);     n0 <- sum(ok & yb == 0L)
  sp <- sqrt(((n1 - 1) * vb + (n0 - 1) * vu) / (n1 + n0 - 2))
  data.table(var = f, auc = a, sep = abs(a - 0.5) * 2,
             cohens_d = (mb - mu) / sp, mean_burned = mb, mean_unburned = mu)
}))
sep[, c("auc","sep","cohens_d","mean_burned","mean_unburned") :=
      .(round(auc,4), round(sep,4), round(cohens_d,3), round(mean_burned,4), round(mean_unburned,4))]
setorder(sep, -sep); print(sep)
       var    auc    sep cohens_d mean_burned mean_unburned

3.2.3 The exact-linear-combination cut (MIRBI + tasseled-cap)

The pairwise pruner is blind to multivariate redundancy: it compares two columns at a time, so it cannot see that a variable is an exact linear combination of several protected ones. Two groups of focal features are exactly that, and they leave the design even though their pairwise \(|r|\) never trips the 0.9 rule:

  • MIRBI \(= 10\,\text{SWIR2} - 9.8\,\text{SWIR1} + 2\) — exactly linear in two bands we keep.
  • TCB, TCG, TCW — exact linear combinations of the six raw optical bands (Baig 2014).

With the raw bands protected, a linear model (and the band×· product terms) already spans these indices: regressing any of them on the bands gives \(R^2 \approx 1\). They add columns and worsen conditioning but contribute no new direction. We verify the exactness two ways — an \(R^2\) from the regression, and the smallest eigenvalue of the relevant correlation submatrix, which is the cleanest fingerprint of rank-deficiency (an exact linear dependence forces an exactly zero eigenvalue).

Code 
r2_on <- function(y, xs) {                      # R^2 of y regressed on columns xs (complete cases)
  M <- as.matrix(dt[, c(y, xs), with = FALSE]); M <- M[is.finite(rowSums(M)), ]
  summary(lm(M[, 1] ~ M[, -1]))$r.squared
}
smallest_eig <- function(vars) {                # min eigenvalue of the correlation matrix
  C <- cor_fast(as.matrix(dt[, ..vars])); min(eigen(C, symmetric = TRUE)$values)
}
exact <- data.table(
  index   = c("MIRBI", "TCB", "TCG", "TCW"),
  spanned_by = c("SWIR1+SWIR2", "6 optical", "6 optical", "6 optical"),
  R2      = c(r2_on("MIRBI", c("SWIR1","SWIR2")),
              r2_on("TCB", c("BLUE","GREEN","RED","NIR","SWIR1","SWIR2")),
              r2_on("TCG", c("BLUE","GREEN","RED","NIR","SWIR1","SWIR2")),
              r2_on("TCW", c("BLUE","GREEN","RED","NIR","SWIR1","SWIR2"))))
exact[, R2 := round(R2, 6)]; print(exact)
    index  spanned_by    R2
   <char>      <char> <num>
1:  MIRBI SWIR1+SWIR2     1
2:    TCB   6 optical     1
3:    TCG   6 optical     1
4:    TCW   6 optical     1
Code

            smallest_eig(c("SWIR1","SWIR2","MIRBI"))))

cat(sprintf("min eigenvalue of cor(6 optical bands + TCB,TCG,TCW) = %.3e  (3 exact deps -> ~0)\n",
            smallest_eig(c("BLUE","GREEN","RED","NIR","SWIR1","SWIR2","TCB","TCG","TCW"))))
min eigenvalue of cor(6 optical bands + TCB,TCG,TCW) = -4.859e-13  (3 exact deps -> ~0)

\(R^2 = 1\) (to floating-point) and a correlation eigenvalue at machine-epsilon confirm exact linear dependence: drop MIRBI, TCB, TCG, TCW. The ash/brightness signal TCB was prized for is not lost — TCB is a fixed weighted sum of the six protected bands, so the model retains full access to that contrast through the bands and their products.

3.2.4 Focal decision — the reduced 11

Combining the pruner with two manual rules (protect one greenness + one moisture index; prefer cheap normalized-difference indices over redundant ones) and the exact-combo cut:

KEEP (11): BLUE GREEN RED NIR SWIR1 SWIR2 (raw optical) · NBR NBR2 (burn) · NDVI (greenness) · NDMI (moisture) · NDSI (the one genuinely independent extra axis, max \(|r|\approx0.54\)).

DROP (10): MIRBI TCB TCG TCW (exact linear combos) · AFRI kNDVI SAVI EVI2 NIRv (greenness/ burn cluster, redundant with NDVI/NBR) · NDWI (McFeeters NDWI \(\approx -\)NDVI, \(r=-0.977\): a greenness axis in disguise, not independent moisture).

Rationale highlights:

  • Greenness = NDVI, not kNDVI: \(r(\text{NDVI},\text{kNDVI})=0.986\), equal separability; NDVI is canonical/cheap and kNDVI’s nonlinearity is recoverable from product terms.
  • Moisture = NDMI, not NDWI/TCW: NDMI is cheaper than TCW, separates better, and \(r(\text{NDMI},\text{TCW})=0.86\) so it covers TCW. We accept one strongly-collinear pair, \(r(\text{NDMI},\text{NBR})=0.966\) — the useful moisture/ash signal is NDMI’s component orthogonal to NBR (ash test: NDMI sep 0.73 vs NBR 0.45), and there is no cheap NIR–SWIR moisture index decorrelated from NBR (they share NIR). This deliberately-kept pair is part of the irreducible near-rank-deficiency analysed in §[VIF].
Code

stopifnot(length(FOCAL_KEEP) == 11)
rm(Mf, Cf_p, Cf_s, A); invisible(gc())
cat("Focal mains kept (11):", paste(FOCAL_KEEP, collapse = ", "), "\n")

These are cheap, only mildly collinear main effects; we keep them generously. (Which prev bands enter the expensive interaction blocks is decided separately, in Step 4.)

3.4 Step 3 — Focal × focal interactions (210 → 22)

With 11 focal mains the pairwise block is \(\binom{11}{2}=55\) candidates (down from \(\binom{21}{2}=210\)). We keep an interaction only if it adds structure beyond the mains and the other kept interactions — pruning by correlation with the 11 mains protected.

Products are built from CENTERED factors, \((X-\bar X)(Y-\bar Y)\), not raw \(X\!\cdot\!Y\) — the only honest way to judge interaction redundancy, since a raw product is mechanically correlated with its parents. Centering the factors genuinely changes the column: \((X-a)(Y-b) = XY - aY - bX + ab\).

Is this just reparameterization? Only without a penalty. In an unpenalized model that also holds \(X\), \(Y\) and an intercept, raw and centered products span the same space → identical predictions. Under glmnet’s penalty it is a different model: the penalty is on the coefficients, which differ between parameterizations for the same surface, so the penalized optimum (selection + shrinkage) differs — in the better-conditioned direction. For deployment the distinction vanishes: once fitted, fold the centering constants into the intercept + main slopes, and GEE deploys raw band products (no means vector).

Code 
OPT_K <- c("BLUE","GREEN","RED","NIR","SWIR1","SWIR2")
IDX_K <- c("NBR","NBR2","NDVI","NDMI","NDSI")
Mk <- as.matrix(dt[, ..FOCAL_KEEP]); Mk <- Mk[is.finite(rowSums(Mk)), ]
Mc <- sweep(Mk, 2, colMeans(Mk), "-")                    # CENTER factors before multiplying
pr <- combn(FOCAL_KEEP, 2)                               # 55 distinct pairs
P  <- vapply(seq_len(ncol(pr)), function(k) Mc[, pr[1, k]] * Mc[, pr[2, k]], numeric(nrow(Mc)))
colnames(P) <- apply(pr, 2, paste, collapse = ":")
Cint     <- cor_fast(cbind(Mk[, FOCAL_KEEP], P))         # raw mains + centered products
drop_int <- find_redundant(Cint, COR_HI, protect = FOCAL_KEEP)
keep_int_pw <- setdiff(colnames(P), drop_int)
blk <- function(t) { ab <- strsplit(t, ":")[[1]]
  if (all(ab %in% OPT_K)) "opt:opt" else if (all(ab %in% IDX_K)) "idx:idx" else "opt:idx" }
itab <- data.table(term = colnames(P), block = vapply(colnames(P), blk, ""),
                   status = fifelse(colnames(P) %in% keep_int_pw, "keep", "DROP"))
cat(sprintf("Pairwise prune: kept %d / 55  (|r| > %.2f, 11 mains protected, centered factors)\n",
            length(keep_int_pw), COR_HI))

3.5 Step 4 — Prev × focal interactions (curated B4–B6, median + sd → 64)

For prev × focal we keep the curated block structure rather than crossing everything: the blocks encode a relevance prior — a band interacts with its own previous-year level (same-band), and previous-year vegetation/fraction state modulates the fire signal — which a pure correlation prune would discard (it removes redundant terms, not useless ones). Two reductions vs the canonical-team blocks: each block uses the median + sd summaries only (dropping \(\text{wet}\approx\text{med}\) and the partly-redundant \(\text{dry}\) from the interactions), and block membership is aligned to the reduced main sets (11 focal, 32 prev).

block prev side (× med + sd) × focal side count
B4 same-band green, nir, swir1, swir2, ndvi each × its own focal band 5 × 2 = 10
B5 idx × fire-idx ndvi, ndwi, npv, ndfi × {NBR, NBR2, NDVI}; skip ndvi×NDVI 4×3×2 − 2 = 22
B6 idx × fire-band ndvi, ndwi, npv, ndfi × {RED, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2} 4×4×2 = 32
total 64

These blocks are not correlation-pruned among themselves — they are already a curated, sparse set. Their multivariate collinearity against the mains is checked next.

3.6 Step 5 — Multivariate collinearity (VIF) and the redundancy we keep on purpose

Pairwise correlation can’t see when a term is a linear combination of several others; VIF can: \(\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R^2_j)\), with \(R^2_j\) from regressing term \(j\) on all others (\(>5\) moderate, \(>10\) serious). It is n-invariant (a function of the correlation matrix only).

The caveat that dominates here, and your question about the bands + ratio-indices. We deliberately keep the 6 raw optical bands and indices that are (near-)functions of them: NBR, NBR2, NDMI are ratios of NIR/SWIR pairs. That makes the protected main set intentionally near-rank-deficient — cor(X) is numerically near-singular, and naïve diag(solve(cor(X))) returns garbage (VIFs in the millions). That collinearity is not a bug and is not removed by deleting terms; it is exactly what the elastic-net ridge component (\(\alpha<1\)) absorbs.

3.6.1 How you see near-rank-deficiency: eigenvalues of the correlation matrix

The clean diagnostic is the eigenvalue spectrum of the correlation matrix of the suspect block. For a set of \(p\) standardized variables, \(\sum\lambda_i = p\). An exact linear dependence forces a \(\lambda_i = 0\); a near dependence forces a \(\lambda_i \approx 0\). The condition number \(\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\) measures how close to singular the block is (\(\kappa \gtrsim 30\) is the usual flag; \(\kappa \gtrsim 1000\) is severe).

Take the block you asked about — {NBR, NBR2, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2}. NBR and NBR2 are ratios built from {NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2}, so five variables live in essentially three underlying dimensions: we expect the two smallest eigenvalues to collapse toward zero and \(\kappa\) to be large.

Code

                 eigenvalue = round(ed, 5),
                 pct_var = round(100 * ed / sum(ed), 2),
                 cum_pct = round(100 * cumsum(ed) / sum(ed), 2)))

5:         5    0.01346    0.27  100.00
Code 
cat(sprintf("\nsum of eigenvalues = %.2f (= p = %d)\n", sum(ed), length(ed)))

sum of eigenvalues = 5.00 (= p = 5)
Code 
cat(sprintf("lambda_max = %.4f,  lambda_min = %.3e\n", max(ed), min(ed)))
lambda_max = 3.2692,  lambda_min = 1.346e-02
Code 
cat(sprintf("condition number  kappa = lambda_max / lambda_min = %.1f\n", max(ed) / min(ed)))
condition number  kappa = lambda_max / lambda_min = 243.0

Read the printed spectrum (full-data values): the first two components carry ~95% of the variance, and the smallest eigenvalue collapses to \(\lambda_{\min}\approx0.013\) — about 240× below \(\lambda_{\max}\approx3.27\), giving \(\kappa\approx243\). That is well past the \(\kappa\gtrsim30\) collinearity flag: five variables effectively live in ~two dominant directions. This is near-rank-deficiency (ill-conditioning), not the exact singularity of §[exact-combo]: there MIRBI / the tasseled-caps drove a correlation eigenvalue to machine epsilon (\(\approx10^{-13}\), an exactly-zero direction) and were removed; here the ratio-indices are non-linear functions of the bands, so the small eigenvalue is small-but-finite — a block we keep and condition with ridge rather than delete.

Why keep a near-singular main block at all? Because (a) the redundancy is not exact — the ratio-indices carry a small but real component orthogonal to the bands (the ash/moisture signal in NDMI⊥NBR is the worked example in Step 1), and (b) dropping a band or a ratio to “fix” the condition number would throw that orthogonal component away. The elastic-net ridge term (\(\alpha<1\)) shrinks along the near-null directions instead of deleting them: it keeps the model identifiable and the fit well-posed without discarding signal. This is precisely why the final \(\alpha\) grid (§[Fitting]) excludes pure lasso (\(\alpha=1\)) — some ridge is needed to condition this block.

3.6.2 VIF used only for the question it can answer: do interactions add anything beyond the mains?

Because the mains are near-singular by design, we use VIF only via a pseudo-inverse to ask: what is the \(R^2\) of each interaction regressed on the main span? (Well-defined even when the mains are collinear.) Mains are never dropped; only interactions are screened.

Code 
PREV_SUMM2 <- c("median","stdDev")
SAMEBAND_K <- c("green","nir","swir1","swir2","ndvi")
CONTEXT_K  <- c("ndvi","ndwi","npv","ndfi")
FIRE_IDX   <- c("NBR","NBR2","NDVI"); FIRE_BAND <- c("RED","NIR","SWIR1","SWIR2")

need <- unique(c(FOCAL_KEEP, PREV_MAIN))
D  <- as.matrix(dt[, ..need]); D <- D[is.finite(rowSums(D)), ]
Dc <- sweep(D, 2, colMeans(D), "-")                              # centered factors

fi  <- strsplit(keep_int_pw, ":")                               # pairwise-kept focal interactions
Xfi <- vapply(fi, function(ab) Dc[, ab[1]] * Dc[, ab[2]], numeric(nrow(Dc)))
colnames(Xfi) <- keep_int_pw

specs <- list()                                                  # prev x focal blocks (median+sd)
for (v in SAMEBAND_K) for (s in PREV_SUMM2)
  specs <- c(specs, list(c(sprintf("mb_mos_%s_%s", v, s), toupper(v))))
for (v in CONTEXT_K)  for (s in PREV_SUMM2) for (f in FIRE_IDX)
  if (!(v == "ndvi" && f == "NDVI")) specs <- c(specs, list(c(sprintf("mb_mos_%s_%s", v, s), f)))
for (v in CONTEXT_K)  for (s in PREV_SUMM2) for (f in FIRE_BAND)
  specs <- c(specs, list(c(sprintf("mb_mos_%s_%s", v, s), f)))
Xpf <- vapply(specs, function(z) Dc[, z[1]] * Dc[, z[2]], numeric(nrow(Dc)))
colnames(Xpf) <- vapply(specs, function(z) paste(z[1], z[2], sep = ":"), "")

X <- cbind(D[, c(FOCAL_KEEP, PREV_MAIN)], Xfi, Xpf)
mains <- c(FOCAL_KEEP, PREV_MAIN); ints <- setdiff(colnames(X), mains)
C  <- cor(X); eA <- eigen(C, symmetric = TRUE)
rk <- function(M){ e <- eigen(M, symmetric = TRUE)$values; sum(e > max(e) * 1e-8) }
cat(sprintf("Assembled design: %d terms (%d main + %d interaction)\n",
            ncol(X), length(mains), length(ints)))
Assembled design: 132 terms (43 main + 89 interaction)

pinv <- ev$vectors %*% ((ifelse(ev$values > tol, 1/ev$values, 0)) * t(ev$vectors))

Reading it (full-data values). The MAIN block is now full rank, 43/43 — dropping the exact-combo indices (MIRBI, TCB/TCG/TCW) restored rank that the canonical-team mains lacked — yet it stays ill-conditioned, the κ≈243 bands + ratio-indices block above. So the residual here is conditioning, not rank-deficiency, and it is left to the ridge term, not removed. The full assembled design printed as 132 terms (43 mains + 89 interactions = the 25 pairwise-kept focal + 64 prev×focal) is rank 131/132 — one interaction is linearly dependent (recip-cond \(\sim10^{-16}\)), which is exactly what the VIF screen catches. At \(R^2_{\text{on mains}}>0.9\) it flags 6 focal opt×idx pairs (NIR:NBR, SWIR1:NBR2, SWIR1:NDMI, SWIR2:NBR, BLUE:RED, NIR:NDVI) that survived the pairwise prune but are multivariately ≥90% reproducible from the mains. None exceed \(R^2=0.95\); production drops the three clearest and keeps three borderline (see Step 3), taking the focal interactions to 22 and the design to its final 129 (43 mains + 22 focal + 64 prev×focal).

4 Part IV — The final design and fitting config

4.1 Final design — before vs after

component canonical-team (427) reduced (129)
focal mains 21 11
prev-year mains 40 32
focal × focal 210 22
prev × focal (B4–B6) 156 64
total terms (+ intercept) 427 129

A ~70% cut (427 → 129), concentrated in the interaction blocks — exactly where coordinate descent was crawling. The block structure used in fitting (workflow/02-model_fitting.R):

Code 
BLOCKS <- c(focal = 11, prev = 32, pairs = 22, sameband = 10, cross_idx = 22, cross_band = 32)
stopifnot(sum(BLOCKS) == 129)
print(as.data.table(as.list(BLOCKS))[, total := sum(BLOCKS)][])
   focal  prev pairs sameband cross_idx cross_band total
   <num> <num> <num>    <num>     <num>      <num> <num>
1:    11    32    22       10        22         32   129

4.2 Fitting config — the convergence fix was numerical

The reduction removes the removable collinearity; the leftover (intentional) collinearity is handled at fit time. The decisive findings, all in 02-model_fitting.R:

  • thresh = 1e-4 (relaxed from glmnet’s 1e-7 default) — the single biggest speed lever. The default tolerance forces coordinate descent to grind out spurious precision in the ill-conditioned low-\(\lambda\) tail; 1e-4 is far below the noise floor of a CV-selected model and converges in a fraction of the iterations. A per-class adaptive fallback loosens further (×5, up to 1e-2) under a wall-clock budget, so no class can stall.
  • nlambda = 50, lambda.min.ratio = 1e-4 — a finer \(\lambda\) path gives better warm starts (each fit initialized from the previous \(\lambda\)); the CV optimum sits near the path floor, so we go deep.
  • \(\alpha\) grid \(\{0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}\) — pure ridge (\(\alpha=0\)) and pure lasso (\(\alpha=1\)) are both dropped: ridge was never best in CV and is slowest, and lasso lacks the ridge component that conditions the intentionally near-singular main block (§[VIF]). The interior keeps that component. Selected at lambda.min (data-rich, near-MLE wanted).
  • Centered-factor interactions, folded back at export — products are fit from mean-centered factors (better-conditioned under the penalty); after fitting, the centering is folded into the intercept + main slopes so the exported coefficients are on the raw-product scale and GEE deploys raw band multiplies (no means vector). Verified numerically (predictions identical) on every fit.
  • CV design — grouped K-fold (\(K=10\), group = region-unique fire id, so whole fires are held out and within-fire temporal autocorrelation cannot leak), folds packed by stratified greedy balancing of obs + positives, pure-negative fires point-distributed across folds, tuned on binomial deviance. Out-of-fold \(p_i\) saved per observation.

With the reduced, conditioned design and the relaxed tolerance, fits that previously ran for hours per \(\alpha\) complete in minutes — confirming the original problem was numerical (ill-conditioning), not statistical.

4.3 GEE computational considerations

The model is evaluated for every Landsat observation in Argentina, 1999–2025. The implementation keeps the GEE compute graph at roughly 15 nodes regardless of term count by expressing each interaction block as one .multiply() between two parallel multiband images, rather than looping per term (which would chain O(n) server-side nodes).

// ---- build the two source images with distinct band names ----
var focal = computeFocal(landsat).rename(focalNames);   // 11 bands, e.g. "NBR_t"
var prev  = mbMosaic.select(prevBandsRaw).rename(prevNames); // 32 bands, e.g. "NDVI_med"
var X0    = focal.addBands(prev);                        // 43 mains

// ---- each interaction block in ONE multiply (parallel band lists) ----
var pairs = X0.select(pairs_a).multiply(X0.select(pairs_b)).rename(pairs_names);     // 22
var same  = X0.select(same_a ).multiply(X0.select(same_b )).rename(same_names);      // 10
var cidx  = X0.select(cidx_a ).multiply(X0.select(cidx_b )).rename(cidx_names);      // 22
var cband = X0.select(cband_a).multiply(X0.select(cband_b)).rename(cband_names);     // 32

// ---- assemble 129-band predictor, weighted sum + sigmoid ----
var X    = X0.addBands(pairs).addBands(same).addBands(cidx).addBands(cband);
var coef = ee.Image.constant(coefValues).rename(coefNames);   // 129 floats, name-matched
var eta  = X.multiply(coef).reduce(ee.Reducer.sum()).add(alpha);
var p    = eta.multiply(-1).exp().add(1).pow(-1);              // sigmoid

The graph size does not grow with the term count: a 500-term version would have the same node count as a 50-term one. Band names must be globally unique (the _t / _med / _sd suffix convention handles it; addBands throws on a clash). SMA-derived layers (NPV, NDFI) are consumed as ordinary mosaic bands — never recomputed per scene — so they cost zero per-pixel array ops on our side. Tasseled-cap, had we kept it, would be one cheap linear .expression(); dropping it nonetheless removes columns that only hurt the fit.

Numerical precision at prediction. GEE uses float32 (~7 significant digits, relative). For \(|\eta|>10\) the sigmoid saturates and precision is irrelevant; near \(\eta=0\) the contributions are by definition not all large, so float32 summation error in \(p\) is \(\sim10^{-5}\) — negligible against downstream smoothing/region-growing. No prediction-time rescaling required. (Optional insurance, if ever needed: a single 32-band centering of the prev mosaic before products, with the means stored in the coefficient JSON; one node, reused across all focal scenes via GEE’s common-subexpression dedup.)

4.4 Summary of design choices

  • Logistic regression: cheap at prediction, trivial in GEE, sufficient when richly parameterized.
  • 11 focal mains + 22 focal pairs: capture non-monotonic fire signatures and disambiguate fire from drought, ash, deforestation, defoliation and agriculture — the dominant Collection-0 confusions — after dropping exact-linear-combo indices (MIRBI, tasseled-cap) that added columns but no information.
  • 32 prev-year mains + 64 prev × focal interactions: turn the focal classifier into a context-aware one without per-pixel temporal-change features.
  • Reduction 427 → 129: removes the removable collinearity (exact dependences, duplicated axes) that made coordinate descent crawl; the irreducible near-rank-deficiency (bands + their ratio-indices) is kept and handled by the elastic-net ridge component.
  • Elastic net \(\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}\), lambda.min, thresh=1e-4: ridge conditions the kept near-singular block; the relaxed tolerance is what actually made fitting fast.
  • No deltas, no annual min/max, no \(\text{dry}\)/\(\text{amp}\) in interactions: absorbed by interactions and the logistic non-linearity, or confounded by the very signal we detect. ```
